hints: First subtract the empty $103 \text{ g}$ beaker from the $361 \text{ g}$ and $351 \text{ g}$ totals to get the true masses of water and oil.
Use $\rho = m/V$ for water with $\rho = 1.00 \text{ g cm}^{-3}$ to find the beaker volume that both liquids share.
Divide the oil mass by that same volume in $\text{cm}^3$ to get oil density in $\text{g cm}^{-3}$ and compare with $1.00 \text{ g cm}^{-3}$.
walkthrough: Find the mass of each liquid by subtracting the beaker: water mass $m_w = 361 - 103 = 258 \text{ g}$ and oil mass $m_o = 351 - 103 = 248 \text{ g}$.
Use density of water to find the beaker volume: $V = m_w/\rho_w = 258/1.00 = 258 \text{ cm}^3$.
The oil fills the same volume $V = 258 \text{ cm}^3$, so apply $\rho_o = m_o/V$.
Substitute values with units: $\rho_o = 248 \text{ g} / 258 \text{ cm}^3 = 0.961 \text{ g cm}^{-3}$.
Since the oil mass is smaller than the water mass for the same volume, its density must be slightly less than $1.00 \text{ g cm}^{-3}$. This is option A.
